# Text as Data: tidytext (todo) {#sec-textasdata}


::: {.callout-note}
**Proposed chapter scope:** Rule- and dictionary-based text analysis with `tidytext`. Covers tokenization, word frequencies, TF-IDF, and dictionary-based sentiment analysis. Deliberately stays at the interpretable/rule-based level.

Topic models (LDA) appear as a *negative example*: bag-of-words topics are lists of words you have to interpret yourself. The modern alternative (embed, cluster, label with an LLM) is in @sec-embeddings.

The chapter ends with document-term counts that are ready to use as features; @sec-ml uses them for a logistic regression.

Include a short callout for readers with their own folder of texts or PDFs, pointing to @sec-readtext.
:::

2. Tokenization. I'd use three levels of "what is a word?" rather than only a non-western example:

Familiar: stopwords, case, punctuation, hashtags and @mentions (which connects back to the ch9 Bluesky data).
Close to home: Dutch or German compounds. Should arbeidsongeschiktheidsverzekering count as one token? Then stemming vs. lemmatization.
Non-western, two kinds:
Languages written without spaces (Chinese, Japanese, Thai). unnest_tokens uses tokenizers, which uses ICU word boundaries through stringi. ICU has dictionary-based segmentation for CJK and Thai, so it produces a segmentation. The interesting question is whether the segmentation is right. This would make a good challenge. It needs checking in webR, because I'm not sure the webR build of stringi includes the full ICU data.
Agglutinative or clitic-heavy languages (Turkish, Arabic wa-/al-). These have spaces, but space-separated chunks are the wrong unit.
n-grams: I'd put them here rather than later, because negation ("not good") is the obvious failure in section 4 and bigrams are the fix.

Dataset
You want two named politicians, modern, redistributable, and in English so students can judge face validity themselves. My preference:

UK Prime Minister's Questions, PM vs. Leader of the Opposition (e.g. Sunak vs. Starmer 2023–24, or Starmer vs. Badenoch 2025).

It's a natural experiment: same venue, same week, the two people speaking to each other. Word-choice differences then reflect position (government vs. opposition) and party rather than setting. That gives a nice substantive question: does Starmer's language change when he moves from opposition to government in July 2024?
Hansard is under the Open Parliament Licence, which allows redistribution with attribution.
There are enough turns for tf-idf by speaker or session and for a small topic model, while staying small enough for webR.
ParlaMint (CLARIN, CC BY) is a related option. It has the same structure for about 29 European parliaments, with UD-lemmatized versions. That gives you a ready-made lemmatization example, plus Turkish or Ukrainian speeches for the "spaces aren't enough" case without leaving the corpus.
Alternatives I considered:

Trump vs. Harris 2024 (debate plus convention speeches) continues ch9's US-election theme. But one debate is thin for tf-idf and topics, and campaign transcripts have murkier licensing than Hansard.
UN General Debate corpus covers every country up to 2024, which suits a non-western angle. But it's countries rather than politicians, and the non-English speeches are translations, which spoils the tokenization point.
Recent SOTUs are public domain and modern up to 2025. But they aren't a real "two politicians" comparison; it's one speech a year.
Dutch debates (e.g. Wilders vs. Timmermans) would link to ch2's election data and give compounds for free. But non-Dutch readers can't judge face validity, and Dutch lexicons are weaker.
If you like the PMQs idea, I can check which ParlaMint-GB or Hansard date range is actually available, and whether stm, topicmodels and ICU-based CJK segmentation work in webR, before you start writing.
